title: Post-Myocardial Infarction Community Secondary Prevention and Cardiac Rehabilitation

evidenceAudit.scope: Adults discharged after a myocardial infarction and followed in primary care: the four secondary prevention drug classes and their duration, monitoring after discharge, cardiac rehabilitation referral and lifestyle advice. Checked against NICE NG185 recommendations 1.3.3–1.3.7, 1.4.1–1.4.42, 1.7.1–1.7.2, 1.8.1–1.8.34 and 1.9.1–1.9.15.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 14 Oct 2026.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: No Saudi post-MI community guideline was opened for this version; the Saudi Heart Association acute coronary syndrome document was used only for the repository's earlier NSTEMI topic and not re-opened. Thresholds and durations are NICE NG185.

NG185 gives no doses for aspirin, the beta-blocker or the ACE inhibitor after MI; aspirin 75 mg and the beta-blocker starting dose come from the repository's earlier topics, and the ramipril dose is the label dose for post-MI heart failure, not for all post-MI patients.

Ticagrelor and clopidogrel doses were reused from the repository's NSTEMI topic (FDA labels) and not re-opened; ticagrelor beyond 12 months (TA420), rivaroxaban (TA335, TA607) and semaglutide (TA1152) are only named, not summarised.
The UK DVLA and Civil Aviation Authority advice in NG185 does not apply in Saudi Arabia; local driving and flying rules were not assessed.
SFDA registration and hospital formulary availability were not independently verified.

pathophysiology.summary: After an MI the risk of a further atherothrombotic event stays high, so four drug classes are offered: an ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelet therapy, a beta-blocker and a statin (NG185 1.4.1). Dual antiplatelet therapy is continued for up to 12 months after MI unless contraindicated, then aspirin alone indefinitely (NG185 1.4.13–1.4.15). A reduced left ventricular ejection fraction changes duration: beta-blocker and aldosterone antagonist benefit continues, and heart failure treatment follows the NICE chronic heart failure guideline (NG185 1.4.31–1.4.32, 1.4.38–1.4.40). Bleeding risk rises with combined antithrombotic therapy, particularly triple therapy with an anticoagulant, so it is assessed at follow-up (NG185 1.4.3, 1.4.21).

symptoms: Recurrent chest pain, breathlessness or palpitations after discharge need review.
Symptoms of heart failure such as breathlessness and ankle swelling (NG185 1.4.38).
Side effects of drugs: cough on an ACE inhibitor, bleeding or dyspepsia on antiplatelets, muscle symptoms on a statin (NG185 1.4.9, 1.4.18).
physicalSigns: Blood pressure and heart rate at each visit (NG185 1.4.2, 1.4.10).
Signs of heart failure on examination.
redFlags: New or recurrent chest pain suggesting a further acute coronary syndrome: emergency assessment.
Hyperkalaemia on an aldosterone antagonist: halve the dose or stop the drug (NG185 1.4.41).
Clinical heart failure with reduced ejection fraction after MI: start an aldosterone antagonist within 3 to 14 days and manage per the NICE heart failure guideline (NG185 1.4.38–1.4.40).
Major bleeding on antithrombotic therapy: urgent review of the antiplatelet and anticoagulant plan (NG185 1.4.21).
precipitants: Missed secondary prevention drugs or stopping dual antiplatelet therapy early (NG185 1.4.15).
Smoking, poor diet, inactivity, overweight and unmanaged hyperglycaemia (NG185 1.3.5, 1.9.1–1.9.15).

differentials.distinguishingFeatures: New chest pain with ECG or troponin change; manage in hospital as an acute coronary syndrome (NG185 1.1–1.2).
Symptoms or signs of heart failure with reduced ejection fraction; add an aldosterone antagonist and follow the chronic heart failure guideline (NG185 1.4.38–1.4.40).

ACE inhibitor cough: switch to an ARB; aspirin intolerance: clopidogrel; beta-blocker unable to continue: diltiazem or verapamil only without pulmonary congestion or reduced ejection fraction (NG185 1.4.9, 1.4.17, 1.4.35).

ruleIn.testName: Blood pressure, renal function and serum electrolytes
ruleIn.modalityTarget: Adult starting or titrating an ACE inhibitor or ARB after MI
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Measure before starting, within 1 or 2 weeks, with each increase and at least annually (NG185 1.4.10).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Detects hypotension, renal deterioration and hyperkalaemia; monitor aldosterone antagonists the same way and halve or stop for hyperkalaemia (NG185 1.4.41).
ruleIn.normalValue: No symptomatic hypotension; creatinine stable and potassium 3.5–5.0 mmol/L

ruleIn.targetCondition: Reduced ejection fraction and heart failure
ruleIn.expectedFinding: Reduced ejection fraction: continue beta-blocker indefinitely, add aldosterone antagonist if heart failure and manage per the NICE heart failure guideline (NG185 1.4.31, 1.4.38–1.4.40).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Determines duration of the beta-blocker and whether an aldosterone antagonist is added (NG185 1.4.29–1.4.33).

ruleIn.modalityTarget: Every adult at the post-MI follow-up appointment
ruleIn.expectedFinding: High bleeding risk favours clopidogrel or aspirin alone in place of ticagrelor and limits combined antithrombotic duration (NG185 1.4.21, 1.4.24).
ruleIn.clinicalRationale: Offer an assessment to all people after MI at follow-up (NG185 1.4.3).
ruleIn.normalValue: Low bleeding risk on the local assessment tool

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Adult with hyperglycaemia after acute coronary syndrome and no known diabetes
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Abnormal results need diabetes management; normal results need at least annual HbA1c or fasting glucose (NG185 1.3.3, 1.3.7).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: HbA1c before discharge; fasting glucose no earlier than 4 days after onset; do not routinely do an OGTT if both are normal (NG185 1.3.3–1.3.4).
ruleOut.normalValue: HbA1c below 5.7% (39 mmol/mol); fasting glucose below 5.6 mmol/L (100 mg/dL)

ruleOut.modalityTarget: Adult after MI on a statin
ruleOut.expectedFinding: Target is LDL cholesterol 2.0 mmol/L or less or non-HDL cholesterol 2.6 mmol/L or less; follow the repository's statin topic for escalation (NG238 1.7.1).
ruleOut.clinicalRationale: Full lipid profile and transaminase 2–3 months after starting and annually thereafter per NG238 (NG185 1.4.42).
ruleOut.normalValue: LDL below 2.0 mmol/L (77 mg/dL) in secondary prevention

references.title: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification
references.edition: NICE NG238, Recommendations 1.7.1 and 1.11.1; cited from NG185 Recommendation 1.4.42

clinicalManagement.title: Check the discharge plan
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At the first primary care contact after discharge
actions: Confirm the discharge summary lists the diagnosis, results, incomplete drug titrations, future plans and secondary prevention advice (NG185 1.7.1).
Confirm a clear plan for further drug titration, blood pressure monitoring and renal monitoring was sent (NG185 1.4.2).

clinicalManagement.title: Continue the four drug classes
actions: ACE inhibitor, titrated to maximum tolerated or target dose within 4 to 6 weeks of discharge and continued indefinitely; ARB if intolerant (NG185 1.4.6–1.4.9).
Dual antiplatelet therapy for up to 12 months, then aspirin indefinitely; clopidogrel if aspirin hypersensitive (NG185 1.4.13–1.4.17).
Beta-blocker titrated to maximum tolerated or target dose (NG185 1.4.27–1.4.28).

clinicalManagement.title: If an anticoagulant is also needed
actions: Weigh bleeding, thromboembolic and cardiovascular risk and the person's wishes (NG185 1.4.21).
After PCI continue anticoagulation and clopidogrel for up to 12 months; do not routinely add prasugrel or ticagrelor (NG185 1.4.22, 1.4.25).
Without PCI continue anticoagulation and consider aspirin for up to 12 months unless bleeding risk is high (NG185 1.4.24).

clinicalManagement.title: Monitor
clinicalManagement.timeframe: 1 to 2 weeks after ACE inhibitor changes; at least annually
actions: Blood pressure, renal function and electrolytes at the intervals above (NG185 1.4.10).
HbA1c or fasting glucose at least annually if hyperglycaemia occurred without known diabetes (NG185 1.3.7).

clinicalManagement.title: Cardiac rehabilitation
clinicalManagement.timeframe: Start before discharge; session within 10 days
actions: Offer a programme with an exercise component to everyone regardless of age (NG185 1.8.1).
Chase non-attenders with a reminder letter, visit or telephone call (NG185 1.8.14).
Offer choice of venue and time, and consider single-sex classes if demand allows (NG185 1.8.9, 1.8.11).

clinicalManagement.title: Lifestyle and recovery advice
clinicalManagement.timeframe: At each visit in the first year
actions: Mediterranean-style diet; no omega-3 capsules or supplements to prevent another MI; no beta-carotene, vitamin E or C, or folic acid supplements (NG185 1.9.1–1.9.5).
Physical activity for 20 to 30 minutes a day to slight breathlessness, built up gradually (NG185 1.9.11).
Stop smoking with support or pharmacotherapy; support weight management (NG185 1.9.13–1.9.15).
Sexual activity can resume when comfortable, usually after about 4 weeks (NG185 1.8.33).

regimens.indication: ACE inhibitor offered after MI as soon as haemodynamically stable, continued indefinitely (NICE NG185 1.4.6–1.4.7)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after MI; the label starting dose below is for post-MI patients with signs of heart failure
regimens.dose: 2.5 mg twice daily; 1.25 mg twice daily if hypotensive; increase after one week toward 5 mg twice daily
regimens.duration: Indefinitely; titrate to maximum tolerated or target dose, completed within 4 to 6 weeks of discharge if not finished in hospital (NG185 1.4.6–1.4.7)
adjustments: Hypotension on the starting dose: switch to 1.25 mg twice daily (label section 2.3)
ACE inhibitor intolerance such as cough: offer an ARB instead (NG185 1.4.9)
Do not combine with an ARB unless there are other reasons (NG185 1.4.8)
monitoring: Renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure before starting and within 1 or 2 weeks, with each dose increase, then at least annually (NG185 1.4.10)
Observe for at least 2 hours after the first dose until blood pressure is stable (label section 2.3)
contraindications: Angioedema with previous ACE inhibitor treatment, or hereditary or idiopathic angioedema (label section 4)
Hypersensitivity to ramipril or another ACE inhibitor (label section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: FDA label version 6, effective 1 July 2022, section 2.3 (Heart Failure Post-Myocardial Infarction) and section 4; indication per NICE NG185 Recommendations 1.4.6–1.4.10

regimens.indication: After MI, continued indefinitely unless intolerant or an anticoagulant is needed (NICE NG185 1.4.13–1.4.14)
adjustments: History of dyspepsia: treat per the NICE dyspepsia guideline (NG185 1.4.18)
Ticagrelor label advises aspirin 75–100 mg daily; the Saudi Heart Association document gives a higher maintenance range (see the repository's NSTEMI topic)
contraindications: Syndrome of asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE NG185 Recommendations 1.4.13–1.4.14 (indication); 75 mg dose from NICE CG126 recs 1.3.3–1.3.5 as reused from the repository's earlier topic

regimens.indication: Second antiplatelet with aspirin after MI, up to 12 months (NICE NG185 1.4.15)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after MI with no separate indication for anticoagulation and no high bleeding risk
regimens.dose: 90 mg twice daily during the first year after the acute coronary syndrome (label); the loading dose is given in hospital
regimens.duration: Up to 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after MI (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.15); label: 90 mg twice daily during the first year after ACS, then 60 mg twice daily
adjustments: Label advises aspirin maintenance 75 to 100 mg daily with ticagrelor, which differs from the SHA aspirin maintenance of 81–162 mg (see comparison)
Do not give with another oral P2Y12 inhibitor (label)
monitoring: Bleeding risk and dyspnoea are not detailed in the cited sections; follow the full label
Single antiplatelet therapy with ticagrelor may be considered after PCI based on thrombotic versus bleeding risk (label section 2.2)
contraindications: Hypersensitivity to ticagrelor or any component (FDA label section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE NG185 Recommendation 1.4.15; FDA label version 23, effective 30 May 2026, sections 2.2 and 4

regimens.indication: Second antiplatelet when anticoagulation is also needed (NG185 1.4.22–1.4.23), or in high bleeding risk; also clopidogrel alone if aspirin hypersensitive (NG185 1.4.17)
regimens.patientGroup: Adults after MI with a separate indication for anticoagulation, or aspirin hypersensitivity
regimens.dose: 75 mg once daily (maintenance after any loading dose given in hospital)
regimens.duration: Up to 12 months of dual antiplatelet therapy after MI; with a new anticoagulant indication after PCI, clopidogrel for up to 12 months (NICE NG185 Recs 1.4.15 and 1.4.23)
adjustments: Starting without a loading dose delays the antiplatelet effect by several days (label section 2.1)
Do not routinely combine prasugrel or ticagrelor with an anticoagulant needed for another indication (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.25)
monitoring: Bleeding risk: triple therapy with aspirin, clopidogrel and an anticoagulant significantly increases bleeding (NICE NG185 Rec. 1.4.21)
contraindications: Active pathological bleeding such as peptic ulcer or intracranial haemorrhage
Hypersensitivity to clopidogrel or any component (FDA label section 4)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE NG185 Recommendations 1.4.17, 1.4.22–1.4.23; FDA label version 18, effective 17 May 2024, sections 2.1 and 4

regimens.indication: Beta-blocker offered as soon as possible after MI when haemodynamically stable (NICE NG185 1.4.27)
regimens.dose: Titrate to the maximum tolerated or target dose per the discharge plan (NG185 1.4.28); the label angina starting dose is 100 mg once daily
regimens.duration: At least 12 months if the ejection fraction is preserved, indefinitely if reduced (NG185 1.4.29–1.4.31)
adjustments: After 12 months without reduced ejection fraction, discuss benefits and risks of stopping or continuing (NG185 1.4.30)
contraindications: Severe bradycardia; second- or third-degree heart block; sick sinus syndrome (without pacemaker)
regimens.sourceTitle: Metoprolol succinate prescribing information (US FDA label, DailyMed)
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE NG185 Recommendations 1.4.27–1.4.33; FDA label as accessed 12 Oct 2026 for the repository's angina topic, Section 2 (Dosage and Administration)

regimens.indication: Statin for secondary prevention after MI (NICE NG185 1.4.42; dose per NG238 1.7.2)
adjustments: Lower dose if interactions, adverse-effect risk or preference
contraindications: Acute liver failure or decompensated cirrhosis
regimens.sourceTitle: NICE NG238: Cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, including lipid modification
regimens.sourceEdition: NICE NG185 Recommendation 1.4.42; NICE NG238 Recommendation 1.7.2

medicationPlan.note: NICE NG185 names the four drug classes and their durations but gives no doses for aspirin, the beta-blocker or the ACE inhibitor after MI (1.4.1–1.4.15, 1.4.27–1.4.31). Aspirin 75 mg and the beta-blocker starting dose are reused from the repository's earlier topics; the ramipril dose is the FDA label dose for post-MI heart failure. Ticagrelor beyond 12 months, rivaroxaban and semaglutide are technology appraisal decisions. SFDA registration was not verified. Check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: Offer an ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelet therapy, a beta-blocker and a statin after MI (NG185 1.4.1)
Up to 12 months after MI unless contraindicated; aspirin alone indefinitely after (NG185 1.4.13–1.4.15)
Consider 12 months if ejection fraction is not reduced; indefinitely if reduced (NG185 1.4.29–1.4.31)
Complete within 4 to 6 weeks of discharge; check renal function, electrolytes and blood pressure within 1 to 2 weeks and then at least annually (NG185 1.4.7, 1.4.10)
Offer to everyone regardless of age; begin before discharge and invite to a session within 10 days of discharge (NG185 1.8.1, 1.8.13)
HbA1c before discharge and fasting glucose from 4 days after onset; offer diabetes testing at least annually (NG185 1.3.3, 1.3.6–1.3.7)

teaching.scope: Adults discharged after a myocardial infarction and followed in primary care: the four secondary prevention drug classes and their duration, monitoring after discharge, cardiac rehabilitation referral and lifestyle advice. Checked against NICE NG185 recommendations 1.3.3–1.3.7, 1.4.1–1.4.42, 1.7.1–1.7.2, 1.8.1–1.8.34 and 1.9.1–1.9.15.
learningObjectives: Name the four secondary prevention drug classes and the duration of each after MI.
Refer to cardiac rehabilitation and give the lifestyle advice NICE recommends.
pitfalls: Stopping the ACE inhibitor titration at discharge and never completing it.
Prolonged triple therapy without a bleeding-risk review.
Recommending omega-3 capsules or vitamin supplements to prevent another MI.
Not chasing patients who miss cardiac rehabilitation.
keyPoints: ACE inhibitor, dual antiplatelet therapy, beta-blocker and statin after MI (NG185 1.4.1).
Dual antiplatelet therapy up to 12 months, then aspirin indefinitely.
Beta-blocker 12 months if ejection fraction preserved, indefinitely if reduced.
Cardiac rehabilitation session within 10 days of discharge.

patientEducation: Explain why each of the four drugs is taken and that the ACE inhibitor and statin are long term (NG185 1.4.6, 1.4.42).
Give the written plan and a copy of the discharge summary (NG185 1.7.2).
Reassure that sexual activity after recovery carries no greater risk of another MI than if the person had never had one (NG185 1.8.32).
lifestyleAndDiet: Mediterranean-style diet with an individual dietary consultation (NG185 1.9.1, 1.9.6).
Physical activity for 20 to 30 minutes a day to slight breathlessness, building up gradually (NG185 1.9.11).
Stop smoking, with referral to a service (NG185 1.9.13).
Healthy weight with support if overweight (NG185 1.9.15).
mdtReferrals: Cardiac rehabilitation team within 10 days of discharge (NG185 1.8.13).
Specialist heart failure team if ejection fraction is reduced (NG185 1.4.40).
Social and welfare support for economic, housing and social issues (NG185 1.8.16).
dischargeCriteria: Discharge summary received with titration plan and secondary prevention advice (NG185 1.7.1).
Cardiac rehabilitation invitation made before discharge (NG185 1.8.13).
Bleeding risk assessed and drug durations written down (NG185 1.4.3, 1.4.15).
nonClinicalManagement.followUpPlan: Follow-up includes a bleeding risk assessment, ACE inhibitor titration within 4 to 6 weeks, renal function and electrolytes at 1 to 2 weeks after each change and at least annually, and a review of antiplatelet and beta-blocker duration at 12 months (NG185 1.4.3, 1.4.7, 1.4.10, 1.4.15, 1.4.29–1.4.30).
